87472.about: Daniel Hajas is an Innovation Manager at University College London, and the director of Project27. At 30 years old, Daniel’s journey from Hungary to becoming a leading figure in disability innovation has been marked by resilience, creativity, and a relentless drive to improve accessibility in science and technology for blind and partially sighted individuals.Born in Hungary, Daniel’s life took a dramatic turn at the age of 16 when he lost his sight. This significant change fuelled his passion for making science and technology accessible to all. Despite the challenges, Daniel pursued his academic interests with determination, moving to Croatia for eight years where he attended an international high school. His love for mathematics and physics then led him to the University of Sussex in England, where he studied theoretical physics.Daniel’s curiosity and solution-focused mindset soon directed him towards the field of accessibility. He began collaborating with charitable organisations such as the IT Foundation for the Visually Impaired, where he played a crucial role in initiatives like the integration of LaTeX Access into e-readers, and the localisation of MathML accessibility in JAWS, a leading screen reader software. These projects significantly enhanced the ability of Hungarian blind and partially sighted individuals to access complex mathematical expressions.In 2017, Daniel’s entrepreneurial spirit led him to co-found a student start-up focused on developing a refreshable tactile graphics display. This venture later pivoted to creating a community-driven solution for providing on-demand descriptions of graphs and diagrams for science students.His growing interest in haptics, human-computer interaction, and science communication spurred him to pursue a PhD in informatics at the University of Sussex, funded by the Bristol-based start-up Ultraleap Limited. His doctoral research contributed to advancements in ultrasonic mid-air haptic technology, enhancing tactile perception and broadening the possibilities for accessible technology.Following his PhD, Daniel began a research collaboration with the MIT Visualisation Group to co-design accessible data visualisations for screen reader users. This work further solidified his reputation as an innovator in accessibility, awarded by the London Business School with an innovation prise. As a result of this research collaboration and open innovation project, Daniel co-founded Project27, a social enterprise building pathways for growth, through co-designing 'solutions that work'. In 2025, MIT CSAIL hosted Daniel as a visiting scientist to further his collaboration with the MIT Visualisation Group.In 2021, Daniel joined the Global Disability Innovation Hub as an Innovation Manager. In this role, as part of the innovation team, he conceptualises, operationalises, and delivers a wide range of projects within GDI Hub's Accelerate programme. His initiatives include early career researcher incubators, which support academic innovators in translating their research into practical applications in assistive technology. Additionally, Daniel leads various work-streams on start-up accelerators across India, East Africa, and the United Kingdom, helping entrepreneurs build sustainable businesses within the disability innovation ecosystem.Outside of his professional life, Daniel is a guide dog owner who enjoys reading books across diverse disciplines, building LEGO sets, and cooking for friends. His multifaceted interests and dedication to improving accessibility continue to inspire and drive meaningful change in the field of disability innovation.
87472.research: My post graduate contribution to science as an early career researcher involves exploring the potential of mid-air haptic technology to enhance public engagement with scientific concepts. Through interdisciplinary research in science communication, haptics, and human-computer interaction, I have developed methods for rendering ultrasonic mid-air haptic shapes that create higher definition tactile perceptions. My work has practical applications in education, such as remote teaching of geometry to blind students, and in enhancing user experiences across various interfaces, including automotive controls and multimedia entertainment. Additionally, I have demonstrated the effectiveness of mid-air haptics in science museums and informal education settings to facilitate multi-sensory learning.Recently, my research has focused on making data visualizations accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) individuals through screen reader technology. As a co-design research collaborator with lived experience of blindness and expertise in human-computer interaction, working with the MIT Visualisation Group I have introduced rich screen reader experiences for accessible data visualization and exploration. This work addresses the lack of comparable non-visual affordances by developing structured, navigable, and descriptive visualizations, which empower BLV users to interact with data at various granularities, enhancing their analytical control and agency. Additionally, I have identified four key design goals for customization: presence, verbosity, ordering, and duration. These principles guided the development of enhanced customization features in the Olli toolkit, improving information identification and memory retention for BLV users. My work on Umwelt, an authoring environment for multimodal data representations, integrates visualization, sonification, and textual descriptions by decentralising the visual modality and creating a representation agnostic grammar of data representations, enabling seamless transitions between these modalities and enhancing data comprehension. The structured editor also addresses design goals of collaboration between sighted and blind people.

87847.about:
From January 2022 to September 2025, Elaine Pimentel was an Associate Professor at the Department of Computer Science at University College London (UCL), UK. She is now a Professor of Logic and Computation at UCL CS!
 
Elaine is also the Treasurer of ACM SIGLOG, Member of the Ethics and Conduct Committee of Brazilian Mathematical Society, Chair of the LA committee of the Association for Symbolic Logic and Chair of the following Scientific committees: TABLEAUX and LFMTP. She was the President (2021-2023) the Treasurer (2023-2025) of the Brazilian Logic Society.Before 2022, she worked as a professor at the Math Departments of the Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG) and the Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte (UFRN), both in Brazil. She has held visiting research positions at TU-Wien (Austria), IRIF and LIX-École Polytechnique (France), and Torino University (Italy). She is the coordinator of Brazilian research projects, and she is part of the European research project MOSAIC (https://sites.google.com/view/mosaic-rise/home). In 2020, Elaine was nominated one of the Ambassadors of Logic in the World Logic day promoted by UNESCO (https://logicday.vcla.at/). Finally, she is and has been co-chair, PC member, organizer of leading conferences in the area of Logic in Computer Science.Her main research interests comprise several aspects of Proof Theory, including: specification and verification of concurrent/computational/logical systems, game semantics, ecumenical logics and proof systems for automatic reasoning.Elaine is also very much interested in all aspects of Diversity and Inclusiveness, working actively in many fronts. Indeed, she is the coordinator of the outreach project POTIMÁTICAS (https://sites.google.com/view/potimaticas/), that aims at encouraging girls to study Mathematics and Computer Science. She runs the platform "Mathematics: feminine noun" (https://matematicasf.wordpress.com/), and she is one of the creators of the collective "Brazilian female logicians" which, among other things, organized the event "Logic and representativeness" (https://logicasbrasileiras.wordpress.com/logica-e-representatividade/). She is also an active member os UCL's Athena SWAN group, where she plans to merge her experience abroad with the wonderful ongoing initiatives developed at UCL. Elaine is very passionate about all the activities she is involved in, and she loves having lively conversations about all of them.

91805.about: Anna is a wheelchair-using activist and researcher whose work spans the disciplines of disability studies, humanitarian relief, international development, urban planning, human-computer interaction, community activism, and social care policy. Recently, she worked with the organization to support Ukrainian disability rights organization Fight for Right in launching an evacuation and humanitarian aid mechanism for disabled Ukrainians being left behind in the international response to the war. In the past, Anna also worked with the Partnership on disability justice-oriented pandemic relief policies and helped to expand the organization's presence in Latin America and the Caribbean. She is currently a Governance Board Member of the UK National Centre for Accessible Transport (ncat) and Trustee for Independent Living Alternatives (ILA).Before this, Anna served the Washington, DC government as a twice-elected Advisory Neighborhood Commissioner. There, she advocated for disability inclusion in DC's urban planning, social care, and pandemic-relief policies. Her achievements included successfully ending the city's de-prioritization of disabled people for COVID-19 vaccines and changing the DC Comprehensive Plan to reflect disability rights frameworks.Anna recieved her BS in Foreign Service (Regional and Comparative Studies, Disability Studies) from Georgetown University and MSc in International Development and Humanitarian Emergencies from the London School of Economics. She grew up in Howell, NJ, USA and is a Truman and Marshall Scholar.Anna's advocacy efforts have been featured in outlets including The New York Times, Washington Post, Forbes, Vogue, and others. She was just named fourth on the Shaw Trust's Disability Power 100, a list of the most influential disabled people in the UK.

93101.about: Elia has a multidisciplinary background. He obtained his BSc in Psychological Sciences from University of San Raffaele in 2008 and his MSc in Cognitive Neuroscience from the same university in 2010. From January 2011 to March 2014 Elia was a PhD student in Design at the Polytechnic of Milan, where he worked within the mechanical engineering department helping developing novel haptic devices for virtual prototyping and assistive applications. During his PhD, from 2012 to 2013, Elia was also a Visiting Researcher at the University of Oxford, where he worked in the psychology department under the supervision of Professor Charles Spence. There, Elia's work focused on evaluating and manipulating customer behavior using multiple sensory feedback. Fascinated by his work in the mechanical engineering department at the Polytechnic school, in 2015 Elia obtained a second MSc in Computational Neuroscience and Cognitive Robotics at the University of Birmingham, while working a sa research associate within the ERC-funded human-robot interaction project “Coglaboration”. His experience on human perception and human-robot interaction allowed him to obtain an internship with Oculus Research in the summer of 2015. In 2016, the company agreed to fund his entire postdoc at University of Sussex, where Elia worked with professor Marianna Obrist investigating mutisensory experiences and emotions in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI). In 2017, Elia moved to the US to work full time as postdoctoral research scientist at Facebook Realty Labs (formerly Oculus research). In 2019 Elia moved back to the UK where he began working as a UX researcher (and later as Behavioural Scientist) for Amazon Text-To-Speech. In this new post, Elia developed an interest towards AI generated content and towards voice perception. Today, since January 2023, Elia is a Lecturer in Computational Design at University College London, as well as a Visiting Academic at Amazon. His research interests include the study of human perception and cognition in the interaction with novel technologies, with a strong accent on VR, AI, and voice interaction.
93101.research: Elia's passion is the study of "what seems real but is not". In Elia's career, this has meant investigating human interactions with novel technologies, including Haptic devices, Virtual Reality, and (more recently) AI agents. Since January 2023, Elia is a Lecturer in Computational Design at University College London (UCL) and an Amazon Visiting Academic (Behavioural sciences). In his post at Amazon, Elia investigates users' perception and cognitive responses to AI voices to inform machine learning engineers and language scientists of opportunities and shortcomings of Text-To-Speech (TTS) models. At UCL, Elia' s research branches towards other "virtual interactions" (that is: interactions designed to feel real, which includes, but it is not limited to, interactions in Virtual Reality). Leveraging on his background in Computational Neuroscience and Cognitve robotics, Elia studies how attention and perception can be manipulated in the virtual environment to deliver novel and immersive experiences to users. These studies include the warping of VR space by manipulating the perceived speed of movement in the virtual environment, the integration of haptic and passive haptic feedback in VR interactions, and the use of AI generated content to drive users' attention during immersive storytelling experiences, the development of haptic devices that "feel human". Elia's research portfolio includes 9 years working and collaborating with for industry.

94770.about: I am an AI researcher dedicated to revolutionizing healthcare by developing self-supervised and foundational AI models that enhance medical imaging, diagnostics, and patient care. With a robust background in deep learning, multimodal data integration, and scalable AI solutions, my work bridges the gap between cutting-edge research and clinical application. During my PhD, I pioneered self-supervised deep learning pipelines for multiclass brain tumor segmentation and prognosis prediction using multimodal MRI data. By integrating imaging features with clinical, demographic, and radiomic information, I enabled robust disease characterization and survival prediction. At University College London, I led the development of BRAINFOUND, a multitasking foundation model capable of segmenting any brain region or pathology, grading tumors, and predicting disease outcomes. Additionally, I developed 3D-SegSync, a self-supervised framework for cardiac and neurological segmentation. Currently, I am advancing multimodal foundation models that integrate MRI, PET, clinical biomarkers, and multi-omics data, facilitating scalable disease characterization and prognosis prediction across diverse clinical applications. My work has been validated in multiple international MICCAI challenges, consistently ranking among the top-performing teams. I have published over 80 papers in peer-reviewed journals and international conference proceedings, contributing to the advancement of AI in healthcare. Beyond research, I am committed to translating AI innovations into clinical practice. I have supervised undergraduate, master’s, and PhD students, led workshops and summer school projects, and collaborated with interdisciplinary teams, demonstrating leadership, mentorship, and collaborative skills. I am particularly motivated to apply my expertise in AI model development and deployment to enhance disease detection, risk stratification, and patient care, contributing to the future of personalized medicine.
94770.research:
AI in Healthcare: Applying deep learning and machine learning to real-world challenges in medical imaging and clinical decision support.
Foundation Models for Medical Imaging: Developing scalable, multitask models trained on large-scale multimodal datasets (MRI, PET, CT, synthetic data) with self-supervised learning for label-efficient adaptation and broad generalizability.
Advanced Medical Imaging: Leveraging MRI, PET, and CT to study neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., Alzheimer’s) and oncological applications (e.g., brain tumors).
Disease Modeling & Prognosis: Designing AI models (CNNs, LSTMs, Transformers) for longitudinal analysis, survival prediction, and disease progression in neurology and oncology.
Multimodal Data Fusion: Integrating imaging with clinical, biomarker, and genomic data to advance personalized medicine and precision diagnostics.
Biomedical Signal & Image Processing: Extracting and analyzing complex features from biomedical data for improved diagnostic insights.
Translational Research: Bridging computational innovations with clinical practice to directly impact patient outcomes.
Generalizable AI Models:  Developing generalizable AI models for diverse medical imaging challenges across multiple organs and modalities  including neuro (stroke, TBI, tumors, fetal brain), cardiac (ventricle, atrial, whole-heart segmentation), fetal & placental imaging, lung disease (pulmonary fibrosis), and systemic conditions (diabetic foot ulcers, COVID-19).

95169.about: I currently hold the position of Professor of Inverse Problems in the Department of Computer Science. Before this, I served as a Senior Lecturer in Inverse Problems and Machine Learning at the School of Mathematical Sciences, as well as an Academic Fellow at the Digital Environment Research Institute, at Queen Mary University of London. My past roles include being a Turing Fellow at the Alan Turing Institute and Director of the Information and Computational Sciences programme at Queen Mary School Hainan. Before I became a lecturer, I was a Leverhulme Trust Early Career Research Fellow, working within Prof. Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb's image analysis group and the Cantab Capital Institute for the Mathematics of Information at the University of Cambridge's Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics. I earned my PhD in Applied Mathematics from the University of Münster, Germany, in 2011, under the supervision of Prof. Martin Burger.My research interests lie in the theoretical and computational aspects of inverse and ill-posed problems, with particular focus on the intersection of inverse problems and deep learning.
95169.research: My research expertise lies in the theoretical and computational aspects of inverse and ill-posed problems. These problems involve deducing unknown quantities—like imaging the interior of a human body—from indirect observations, which is achieved by inverting a mathematical operator. This inversion process is typically unstable, especially when faced with measurement errors. To counter this, the inverses can be approximated through a series of continuous operators, known as regularisation operators. My research primarily focuses on exploring and implementing both model-based and data-driven regularisation methods. This involves a profound understanding of nonlinear regularisation theory coupled with machine learning. My interdisciplinary approach integrates various fields such as numerical analysis, optimisation, deep learning, functional analysis, compressed sensing, and data analytics, to address these complex problems.My research interests include but are not limited toInverse problemsRegularisation theoryMachine learningImage processingImagingOptimisation

96949.about:
George Chalhoub examines the societal impacts of AI, with a focus on the privacy and security risks created by LLMs. His research explores how design practices, legal frameworks, and UX intersect to expose sensitive information, and how law, cybersecurity, and HCI safeguards can reduce these risks.
 
He is a faculty member in Human–Computer Interaction at the UCL Interaction Centre (UCLIC), a Faculty Associate at the Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society at Harvard Law School, and an Associate Member of the Department of Computer Science at the University of Oxford.
His projects have included work on copyright takedown systems, the security of NHS health records, and the design of privacy-friendly technologies for children’s apps. His current agenda extends this trajectory to the risks of prompt disclosure in LLMs, exploring how technical, legal, and UX interventions can mitigate emerging forms of exposure.
George completed his DPhil in Cyber Security at the University of Oxford, funded by the UK Information Commissioner’s Office. He is also the recipient of a UK Global Talent Visa awarded by UKRI.
96949.research:
George’s main research interests focus on the security and privacy of AI systems, with a particular emphasis on how design, governance, and user experience shape risks and protections. His work examines both technical vulnerabilities and human-centred consequences, aiming to build safeguards that make AI safer, fairer, and more trustworthy.
Key areas of interest include:

Security and privacy in LLMs and generative AI: investigating prompt disclosure risks, unintended data exposure, and model exploitation.
User experience of AI security: studying how people interact with AI systems, how misconceptions create new vulnerabilities, and how interfaces can be redesigned to protect sensitive data.
AI governance and legal frameworks: analysing how regulation, platform policy, and institutional practices affect privacy and accountability in AI deployment.
Risks to vulnerable groups: exploring how marginalized communities, online creators, and data workers are disproportionately exposed to AI-driven harms.
Human-centred safeguards: developing technical, legal, and UX-based interventions that reduce misuse and increase resilience across critical domains such as healthcare, law, and journalism.

He is the co-author of 20+ conference, patent, and journal publications.

These models offer unparalleled context-awareness in a zero-shot manner, enabling intelligent behaviour without task-specific training. My work addresses the significant challenges of deploying these foundation models in diverse and unpredictable environments, focusing on three key areas:
 

Generalization Across Modalities – Ensuring robust performance of AI models across various sensors used by different agents.
Computational Efficiency – Optimizing foundation models to run effectively on limited hardware resources.
Human-Machine Interaction – Facilitating seamless and intuitive interactions between AI systems, human users, and other machines.

 
At the core of my research is the mission to enable embodied AI systems to operate reliably in real-world settings.

I am invested into understanding how AI can be used to improve systems security tasks, with a particular emphasis on settings in which attackers adapt quickly to new defenses. I also care deeply about the practicality of our proposed solutions, and on understanding implications and limitations of using AI in the context of computer security. To this purpose, I also regularly engage and collaborate with industry. I mostly work on malware analysis and network traffic, but I am becoming more interested in understanding inner workings of AI and ML models to improve their trustworthiness in more general security scenarios.

100115.about:
I’m an Associate Professor at UCL, where I study how animals achieve agility and speed and then apply those insights to robotics. My background is in mechatronics engineering, and I began my career as a flight control engineer before moving into animal biomechanics. Over time, my work has expanded to include sensor fusion, computer vision, and optimal control—all aimed at measuring and modeling locomotion in real-world conditions.
I collaborate with conservationists, biologists, and fellow engineers to understand factors like spine flexibility and tail dynamics in animals. In parallel, I translate those biological principles into more capable robots, focusing on practical applications in fields such as ecology, disease monitoring, and sports science. My research has been recognized by awards such as the Google Research Scholar Award and the MathWorks Research Award, but my main motivation is to uncover how living systems move and adapt, and to channel that knowledge toward useful, real-world technologies.
100115.research:
Sensor FusionMy work centers on capturing the motion of wildlife in ways that are both detailed and non-invasive. I fuse data from a range of sensors—high-speed cameras, inertial measurement units (IMUs), lidars, and even event cameras—to create precise, 3D representations of animal movement in natural environments. By using advanced AI algorithms to combine these diverse sensor streams, I aim to unlock hidden aspects of locomotion and behavior that were previously too difficult or risky to measure.
Bio-Inspired RoboticsI develop novel robotic systems as physical models that mirror key biomechanical features of animals. By studying how cheetahs and other species accelerate, turn, or stabilize themselves, I can translate these biological strategies into robotics hardware. This approach not only sheds light on the fundamental principles of animal biomechanics but also drives the creation of agile, versatile robots capable of performing rapid maneuvers across complex terrains.
Trajectory Optimisation & ControlTo understand the neuromechanics of locomotion—and to guide robotic control—I develop and apply trajectory optimisation techniques that incorporate contact dynamics and real-world constraints. These methods allow me to simulate, predict, and refine movements in both animals and machines. By integrating sensor-derived data with control algorithms, I’m able to piece together how nervous systems might coordinate muscles and limbs, ultimately enabling robots to move with agility and resilience inspired by the animal kingdom.

My research lies at the intersection between Quantum Machine Learning and Tensor Networks, using methods involving the latter in order to find potential quantum advantage in the former. 101882.research:
My research is focused on applying tensor networks (TNs) to machine learning — both classical and quantum — in order to provide alternative models that would replace neural networks. There are two main reasons for this specific target. Firstly, TNs can be naturally translated to quantum circuits. This can lead to quantum algorithms that benefit from the particular structure brought by the TNs. Secondly, any algorithms involving TNs benefit from a reduction in the number of parameters, which can lead to a decrease in energy and storage cost.
 
My doctorate involves working in applications such as image and language tasks, e.g. the use of grammar as means to construct tensor network layouts for classification algorithms. This involves Python packages such as lambeq. However, I also aim to consider theoretical approaches to proving quantum advantage in the context of machine learning.
 
I am also interested in viewing tensor networks from a geometric perspective, and thus what would the "geometry" of language look like based on different mathematical models for grammar (such as Lambek calculus).

I am a Lecturer (aka. Assistant Professor) at the Centre for Research on Evolution, Search, and Testing (CREST) in the Department of Computer Science at University College London.
 
My research builds the next generation of coding agents that work like software engineers inside a real command-line environment, reasoning across an entire codebase and its tools to tackle tasks such as issue resolution, agent failure repair, and more. My group focuses on CLI coding agents: we design the agent harnesses they operate in, train them in realistic terminal-world environments, and study why they fail and how they can repair themselves. What I care about most is making these agents secure and cost-efficient, so that they are actually affordable in practice. We also maintain Awesome Code Agents, a curated list of cutting-edge coding-agent projects and research.
 
Prior to joining UCL, I worked as a Postdoctoral Researcher at Carnegie Mellon University with Prof. Claire Le Goues. I obtained my PhD from KTH Royal Institute of Technology, where I was fortunate to be supervised by Prof. Martin Monperrus and Prof. Benoit Baudry. I received my bachelor’s degree from Sichuan University.
 

Funding: We greatly appreciate that our research is supported by Google, AWS, Mistral AI, etc through computing credits and gift funding.
102291.research:
My research centers on advancing AI-driven software engineering by building rigorous benchmarks and sophisticated agents capable of navigating complex, real-world development workflows.
 
TerminalWorld: Benchmarking Agents on Real-World Terminal Tasks
TerminalWorld is a benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on the everyday terminal workflows executed by developers. Its primary novelty lies in an automated pipeline that mines real terminal recordings to create reproducible, test-verified task environments that automatically stay live as software engineering practices evolve.
 
ContextBench: A Benchmark for Context Retrieval in Coding Agents
ContextBench focuses on evaluating how coding agents perform multi-file context retrieval across an entire software repository. Its core novelty is measuring the granular dynamics of retrieval—evaluating not just whether the correct files are identified, but also the context F1 accuracy, efficiency, and computational cost required for agents to gather that context.
 
Prometheus: Towards Long-Horizon Codebase Navigation for Repository-Level Problem Solving
Prometheus introduces a specialized coding agent tailored for repository-level problem solving capable of navigating large codebases over extended horizons. Its novelty stems from unifying embedding-based retrieval, structure-aware knowledge-graph navigation, and a dynamic working memory over the agent's trajectory, enabling it to successfully gather context across multiple files and reasoning steps to achieve top-tier results on benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified and SWE-PolyBench.

I investigate hardware–software co-design approaches for intelligent autonomy, including the use of Focal-plane Sensor-Processor Arrays (FPSPs) to enable ultra-high-speed low-power perception and processing. 103833.research:
Preetham Nagaraj’s research interests center on developing physical, tangible technologies to address mental health challenges, particularly trauma recovery in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). He is passionate about creating assistive technologies that integrate psychology, tangible interfaces, mindfulness, and Indic worldviews to support healing. His work focuses on designing tactile, body-centric devices that deliver sensory-driven interventions, fostering emotional regulation and resilience in culturally diverse settings like Nepal. By combining these elements, he aims to bridge mental health gaps with innovative, accessible tools.
 
Beyond tangible technologies, Preetham explores how indigenous worldview can be applied to human-computer interaction (HCI). He investigates the role of community-driven design in ensuring technologies reflect local values, enhancing their effectiveness. His interdisciplinary approach seeks to advance assistive technology by merging psychological insights with cultural narratives, paving the way for impactful mental health solutions.

I am a PhD researcher at UCL in the EIGENDATA project, working on the theoretical and computational study of eigenvector statistics in random matrix ensembles and their applications in machine learning. My work focuses on bridging random matrix theory and modern learning systems, with a particular interest in training dynamics and the spectral structure that lies beyond eigenvalues.
I am especially interested in how eigenvectors of key matrices such as the Hessian in neural networks evolve during training, and what they reveal about optimisation behaviour and generalisation. More broadly, my research combines analytical results, numerical simulations, and spectral methods to develop tools for understanding learning dynamics and closing the gap between idealised theoretical models and more realistic machine learning settings.

105497.about: I am a PhD student at the Robotics-Enabled Biology Lab (REBL) and the Robot Perception and Learning (RPL) Lab, Department of Computer Science, University College London. My PhD research aims to understand animals through robotics. I am particularly interested in how cheetahs optimize stability, efficiency, and agility in their movement. To study this, I am exploring Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) and Inverse Optimal Control (IOC) as tools to uncover the principles underlying cheetah locomotion. More broadly, I envision robotics as a scientific method to investigate animal biomechanics, bridging neuromechanics, control theory, and biorobotics to gain new insights into locomotor strategies in nature. My PhD research is funded by MathWorks.Before joining UCL, I was a Robotics Research Engineer at EPFL, Switzerland, for my master's valorisation. I earned my Master of Research degree in Medical Robotics with Distinction from the Hamlyn Centre for Robotic Surgery at Imperial College London. I am grateful to be supported by Chiang Chen Foundation and Imperial College during my master's degree. Prior to Imperial, I spent my last year undergraduate at ETH Zurich, Switzerland, mainly for my bachelor's thesis. I obtained my Bachelor of Engineering degree in Automation from Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin, China, in June 2023, with a semester abroad at KTH and a year abroad at ETH Zurich, and with the highest honor "Top Ten Outstanding Graduates of Harbin Institute of Technology".
105497.research:
